metaData.originalTitle: Auto Research 时代，47 个没有标准答案的任务成了 Agent 能力必测榜
metaData.title: The Era of Auto Research: 47 Tasks Without Standard Answers Become the Ultimate Test for Agent Capabilities
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: Frontier-Eng Bench systematically tests AI Agents' long-term iterative optimization capabilities in real-world environments through 47 engineering optimization tasks without standard answers, revealing evolutionary patterns of power-law decay and the superiority of depth over breadth.
metaData.summary: This article introduces the Agent Benchmark — Frontier-Eng Bench — released by Navers lab under Einsia AI, designed to evaluate AI Agents' continuous optimization capabilities in real engineering scenarios. Unlike traditional coding problems or knowledge-based Q&A, this benchmark comprises 47 interdisciplinary hardcore tasks spanning areas such as underwater robot stability, lithium plating boundaries in power batteries, and quantum circuit noise control. Agents must complete a full engineering loop: proposing solutions, interfacing with simulators, receiving feedback, modifying parameters, and re-running. Test results show that GPT-5.4 performs most consistently overall, but all models still fall far short of "mastering" the benchmark. The research team identified two key patterns: the frequency and magnitude of improvements follow a power-law decay with each iteration round (the harder it gets to improve over time), and while parallel exploration (breadth) is useful, deep iterative optimization is indispensable. This benchmark marks a paradigm shift for AI from a "one-shot answer" model to a "system capable of continuous iterative evolution through long-term feedback," suggesting that the era of Auto Research may be accelerating.

mainPoints.point: Frontier-Eng Bench tests AI's continuous optimization ability through 47 engineering tasks without standard answers.
mainPoints.explanation: Tasks include underwater robot control, battery fast-charging optimization, and quantum circuit noise control, requiring Agents to iterate autonomously in simulation environments rather than solving problems from memory.

mainPoints.point: The frequency and magnitude of AI improvements follow a power-law decay with each iteration round.
mainPoints.explanation: Early iterations yield quick "low-hanging fruit," but improvements become increasingly difficult and smaller in magnitude over time, closely mirroring real-world R&D processes.

mainPoints.point: Parallel exploration (breadth) is useful, but deep iterative optimization is indispensable.
mainPoints.explanation: Exploring multiple paths can prevent deadlock, but with a fixed budget, breadth often compromises depth; true engineering breakthroughs rely on sustained accumulation and structural leaps.

mainPoints.point: This benchmark marks a paradigm shift for AI from "one-shot answers" to "long-term iterative evolution."
mainPoints.explanation: Agents are no longer just auxiliary tools; they continuously optimize in real feedback loops like professional engineers, signaling the potential acceleration of the Auto Research era.

keyQuotes: If you throw an AI into an engineering scenario without standard answers, can it survive?
Real engineering optimization is never about multiple choice; there is no single standard answer.
Truly advanced intelligence fundamentally relies on long-term feedback loops.
Anyone can produce a first version; the real challenge lies in that final 1% performance leap.
When AI learns to 'optimize over the long term,' how far is it from true engineering intelligence?

relatedArticles.title: The Second Half of Large Model Architecture
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article proposes that large model architecture has entered a second half centered on 'scaling communication,' critiques the traditional 'accumulation' paradigm of residual connections, and introduces innovative solutions for inter-layer 'selective retrieval' through Flash Depth Attention and MoDA.
